stat_summary: Of all UK higher education students in 2023/24, 57% were female and 43% were male, a split that has been unchanged since 2016/17, according to HESA. The gap is widest on other undergraduate courses and narrowest on postgraduate research courses.
stat_source_title: Higher Education Student Statistics: UK, 2023/24, HESA

male.headline: The Girls + Callum: Men Are Just 43 Per Cent of University Students, and He's Been Put in Charge of the HDMI Cable
male.standfirst: New official figures confirm what every bloke already knows from a seminar that leans one way, a group chat with an unfortunate name, and the question of whether he is in the wrong room.
male.image_caption: Callum, 20, keeping a seat warm for a cohort that has not, as yet, arrived.
body_paragraphs: New official figures have confirmed what every bloke already knows from a lecture theatre that leans one way: men are now clearly the minority in British higher education. Only 43 per cent of students in 2023/24 were male, against 57 per cent female, a split that has not shifted since 2016/17, and the main official response, so far, has been to hand the remaining lad the HDMI cable.

“Our group chat is called ‘the girls + Callum’,” said Callum, 20, from Hull. “I have been put in charge of the HDMI cable. Nobody has asked where the other lads went, but they have asked me to move a table.”

The same HESA statistics show the gap is even wider on other undergraduate courses, which rather suggests the missing men are not all off doing doctorates. Campaigners are already calling for a careers talk in every school that does not, in their words, “assume the boys will be fine”, and for a spare chair that is not immediately used as a bag.
Yet where is the outrage? Where is the documentary? Britain’s scarce undergraduate male opens his notebook, alone, with only a rucksack on the next chair for company.
male.pull_quote: Our group chat is called ‘the girls + Callum’. I have been put in charge of the HDMI cable.

female.headline: Submitted at 11.58pm: 57 Per Cent of Students Are Women, and They Also Booked the Room
female.standfirst: Official statistics have finally measured who is actually doing the degrees, and it does not look like a lad-heavy campus from a 1990s prospectus, or a fair division of the group project.
female.image_caption: Maya, 22, still in the library. The dissertation has not, at any point, marked itself.
body_paragraphs: Official statistics have at last measured who is actually doing the degrees. Fifty-seven per cent of UK higher education students in 2023/24 were women – a 14-point gap that has been stable for years – which means the lecture theatres, the libraries and, above all, the group projects are, in any honest count, being propped up by them.

“He added one slide, called himself ‘team lead’ on LinkedIn, and went to the pub,” said Maya, 22, from Leeds. “I wrote the literature review, booked the room and submitted it at 11.58pm. The slide was in Comic Sans.”

Researchers note that women are the majority at almost every level of study, so this is not a blip in a single subject, or a one-off booking of a seminar room. Campaigners are demanding a Group Project Credits Act and a national apology for the phrase “you’ll be fine, girls always do the work”.
Until then, the country’s unofficial first-class majority will keep a seat in the library, one overdue chapter at a time.
female.pull_quote: He added one slide, called himself ‘team lead’ on LinkedIn, and went to the pub.
